And no one more so than Diane Sawyer. Now 68, Sawyer, the oldest of the three women by more than a decade, has enjoyed the most enduring and versatile career, as a brilliant investigative reporter, interviewer and anchor, who mastered both morning and evening news. This erudite former beauty queen was born in Kentucky to a revered judge and an exacting mother, both survivors of Depression-era poverty. She became the first full-time female TV news reporter in Louisville before moving to Washington, where she landed a position in the press office of Richard Nixon’s White House — and stayed with Nixon years after he resigned, to help him write his memoirs.
That culturally dissonant loyalty put off her new colleagues when she finally nabbed a job at CBS’s Washington bureau in 1978 — Lesley Stahl threatened to quit in protest, an insider recalls — but she was savvy enough to know she had to prove herself to defuse the animus, and willingly took on “crap duties” (in the words of a CBS veteran) until she earned everyone’s respect. She quickly established herself as a workhorse with her coverage of three major stories: the Jonestown massacre, Three Mile Island and the Iranian hostage crisis.
But the workhorse was also a tireless perfectionist: Sawyer called her “beleaguered” staff at all hours and “intensely micromanaged” stories up until the last minute before airtime, her rigor improving the quality greatly but at times yielding mistakes. As if compelled, Weller digs into her reputation within the industry for being “manipulative” and calculating: “The chief term applied to her . . . is ‘leaves no fingerprints.’ ” But while “she
thinks
she doesn’t leave fingerprints,” one former colleague tells Weller, “she leaves
cat paw
prints on people’s foreheads.” Another says, “She’s playing three-­dimensional chess while you’re
sleeping
.”
Being critical of Sawyer appears to be painstaking work for Weller; so does praising Couric, who is cast as the consummate opportunist. Still, the author gives grudging credit to her quick wit, keen instincts and tenacity. Like Amanpour, Couric worked at CNN early in her career. But she cut her teeth at NBC reporting on Operation Desert Shield from Saudi Arabia (the two women shared quarters), where she “advanced her lifelong effort to be taken seriously.” She served as a correspondent at the Pentagon before landing on the “Today” couch beside the irascible Bryant Gumbel, whom she’d regularly keep in check. “Being a morning anchor,” Weller explains, “is like being an actor playing a half-dozen different characters in a two-hour-long one-man stage show. Katie just had a knack for it, and its built-in ironies matched her wit.” A clever, pugnacious interviewer, like Sawyer, Couric could draw out politicos as authoritatively as she could soothe people who were grieving — a talent, Weller notes, that Amanpour lacked, which may have contributed to her failure as a network anchor.

Weller has only awe for Amanpour, the daughter of a wealthy Muslim Iranian and a Catholic Englishwoman. She herself has said, “I had to lose the ability to hear the word ‘no,’ ” after CNN refused to allow the fearless, hungry journalist to appear in front of the camera because of her foreign accent, her black, “unruly” hair and her name, which was “too unpronounceable” — even as her skill set (including a knowledge of Farsi) was increasingly in demand. It’s impossible not to be in awe: Amanpour, who was almost killed by the Taliban, transformed war reporting into a mission in an effort to seize Americans’ attention, invite their sympathy, incite their rage to help propel our government into action. And she extended that further by using her journalism as a means to seek social justice for women and children in dire need around the world.
If Weller subjects these women to a double standard, she periodically checks in with herself: Were the top male anchors capable of backbiting? Absolutely. Dan Rather, a producer tells her, “would kill Tom Brokaw and Peter Jennings, and vice versa.” A CBS reporter says, “Dan would kill
anybody
who looked like he wanted his job.” Weller notes that these stories rarely if ever made the tabloids, unlike the fabricated “catfights” among female anchors. To explain the women’s machinations and motivations, she offers more than a few cautionary tales, like that of Jane Pauley, who was anything but a tough negotiator and got pushed aside as a result.
So it’s hard to come away from “The News Sorority” feeling anything less than admiration, if not reverence, for Couric, Sawyer and Amanpour, and sympathy for all the women — from trailblazers like Walters and Stahl to those who never quite broke through (Deborah Norville, the tragic Jessica Savitch) — who had to wrangle with ratings, network politics and defiantly sexist executives, while managing the delicate egos of their male counterparts. And that is, in the words of the old CBS slogan, “very good news.”

Diane Sawyer, Katie Couric, Christiane Amanpour — and the (Ongoing, Imperfect, Complicated) Triumph of Women in TV News
By Sheila Weller

India’s sliver of the Francophonie, the region where French is still the official language, occupies a grid of tree-lined boulevards just south of city of Chennai along the Coromandel Coast, facing east toward the Bay of Bengal. Streets bear names like Rue de la Campaigne and Rue Labourdonnais. Buildings in the White Town (also called the French Quarter) are still graced with long verandahs and elegant compound walls, a genteel French-colonial vision straight out of Indochina, inflected with the pastel calm of India’s palm-fringed south. Since 2006 the town has officially been known as Puducherry, but most people here and across India still call it by its original name, Pondicherry, or its loving diminutive, Pondy.
Sylvaine Ségiyane Paquiry was born and raised in Pondy, attending the French School until 1991 when he left India and moved to France with his parents. He returned to his hometown in 2006 and within a year had opened
La Villa Shanti
, a midrange boutique hotel in the city’s gracious heritage quarter. Eight years later, he has opened the doors to his second property there,
La Villa
, Villa Shanti’s luxury cousin (he has been invited to apply for membership in the international consortium of boutique hotels and restaurants, Relais & Chateau, which first entered India in 2008). Though they target different audiences, both properties share the same principles of “transparency, honesty, simplicity.”
Working with Tina Trigala and Yves Lesprit, the same team of French architects that designed Villa Shanti, Ségiyane has approached La Villa as an exercise in adaptive reuse and heritage conservation. “Most people who own old colonial or Tamil houses have no choice but to demolish or sell, so the old colonial houses are threatened,” he says. For La Villa, the team has taken a long-term lease on a 19th-century home called Villa Notre Dame de la Garde and transformed it into an intimate, six-bedroom hotel that combines a respect for the building’s heritage with a clear-eyed approach to contemporary design.
Wherever possible, the original features of the building have been preserved, while in the newer portions of the hotel Trigala and Lesprit have worked with more modern materials to highlight the differences in period and style, rather than mask them behind a faux-heritage veneer. The lobby maintains the original ceiling beams and columns while replacing the floors with concrete and cement tile, sympathetic to, but careful not to imitate, the original building’s style. In the bedrooms and bathrooms, imported French linens and toiletries from Fragonard are matched with humble bamboo accents from local markets. Doors in the newer part of the hotel have been fashioned from old teakwood doors sourced from the city’s antiques markets. “How we’ve managed to match the two, the future and the past, is what sets us apart — how we’ve given another life to these popular items from the street,” says Ségiyane.
When it opens officially on August 1, La Villa will have a rooftop swimming pool, a small boutique selling items sourced from around town and designed by the architects and a 12-table garden restaurant serving simple cuisine inspired by ingredients produced nearby (the proximity of the organic farms and cheesemakers at Auroville will make for an unusually broad selection). In the coming years, Ségiyane hopes to see La Villa and La Villa Shanti expand to other cities and towns across India, taking with them their ethos of “strong local identity” and a pared-down vision of luxury disconnected from the marble and gilt that dominate the country’s five-star properties.
“Our vision of luxury is space, pleasure for the eye,” Ségiyane says. “It’s something that you don’t see every day.”

A large review of available data has confirmed what many experts have long suspected: Taking small amounts of aspirin over long periods of time reduces the risk of colon cancer and certain other cancers.
British researchers gathered evidence from six published systematic reviews and four individual studies with data on long-term aspirin use in people  50 to 65.
The analysis,
published online in Annals of Oncology
, found strong evidence that aspirin reduced the risk for colorectal cancer, and good evidence that it also reduced the risk for esophageal and stomach cancers. There were smaller or more variable effects for protection against breast, prostate and lung cancers.
They also found that long-term use was required. In controlled trials, there was no benefit until at least three years of use, and mortality was reduced only after five years. A “baby aspirin” of 75 to 81 milligrams was sufficient, and there was no evidence that larger doses provided added benefit.
Gastrointestinal bleeding was a common and serious side effect, and the risk increases with age. But “there was clear evidence that the benefits vastly outweigh the side effects,” said the lead author, Dr. Jack Cuzick, the director of the Wolfson Institute of Preventive Medicine at Queen Mary University of London. “People should talk to their doctors to make sure there’s no risk of bleeding, but the evidence is that everyone between 50 and 65 should consider aspirin.”
